findings.location: Table 2, No limitations / Veteran vs Nonveteran, Suicide attempt
findings.notes: The CI implies p = 0.935 against a printed p = .92. The gap is 0.015 on a null result and is well within what 2-decimal rounding of the AOR (implied centre 0.977) and of both CI bounds can produce. No substantive consequence: non-significant on either reading. Reported for completeness, not as an integrity signal.

findings.location: Table 2, Veteran / >=3 Limitations, Suicidal ideation only
findings.notes: The interval implies p = .0024, roughly 2.4x LARGER than the printed threshold of <.001. Contrast the neighbouring cell 2.60 (1.59-4.24), whose interval implies p = .00013 and genuinely clears <.001. The estimate and interval are mutually consistent; it is the p-value LABEL that does not follow from them. A design-based t reference distribution cannot account for a gap this size at NSDUH's large design df. Substantively harmless (significant either way), but it is a printed p that its own interval does not support. Note: stalt_check was also run here and returned 'consistent', but STALT tests only whether a hidden p is suspiciously SMALL and so does not adjudicate this direction; the finding rests on the check_estimate_ci recovered p.

findings.location: Table 2, 2 Limitations / Veteran vs Nonveteran, Suicide planning
findings.notes: The tool attached a note that this interval 'behaves like a 90% CI, not the stated 95%'. That is an artefact of the estimate being printed as 1.03 while the interval's geometric centre is 1.035; with a near-null OR and 2-decimal rounding the alternative-level test is unstable. findings.location: Table 3, all 20 non-reference AOR (95% CI) cells
findings.quote: 1 Limitation 0.49 (0.24 to 0.97)c .04 ... 2 Limitations Veteran 0.31 (0.14 to 0.66)c .002
findings.notes: 8 of 20 Table 3 odds ratios show a small disagreement between the printed p and the p recovered from the interval. Every discrepancy is <= 0.012 in absolute terms and none changes a significance call (0.49 -> .0453 and 1.61 -> .0344 remain significant; the rest remain non-significant). All 20 estimates sit correctly at the geometric centre of their own intervals. This is the signature of rounding: Table 3's ORs and CI bounds are printed to 2 decimals on small values, so the recovered SE is coarse. Denominator context: 9 of the 50 odds ratios across both tables (18%) show such sub-0.02 drift, consistent with rounding rather than an integrity problem.

findings.location: Results, 'Suicide Ideation, Planning, and Attempt by Veteran and Disability Status', final sentence
findings.quote: No significant differences in risks for suicide were observed by veteran status among people reporting 3 or more disabling limitations.
findings.notes: Produced by absence_of_evidence (recorded under 'reconcile', the nearest schema term). The paper converts a non-significant result into a statement of no difference. The interval for the >=3-limitation veteran-vs-nonveteran attempt contrast still permits a 3.1-fold effect in either direction - compatible with veterans having roughly one third the odds, or triple the odds, of attempt. Companion contrasts in the same stratum are similarly wide (ideation 0.58-1.58, planning 0.65-2.03). The tool declines to judge equivalence because no smallest effect size of interest is stated anywhere in the paper, and that refusal is the correct result: this stratum is uninformative rather than null. Relevant to the abstract's framing, since >=3 limitations is the most severely disabled group.

findings.location: Methods, Statistical Analysis vs Tables 2 and 3
findings.quote: Multivariable adjusted multinomial logistic regression with an interaction term for disability status x veteran status estimated adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% CIs for suicide ideation, planning, and attempt by disability and veteran status.

inputs.claim: veteran status moderates the disability-suicide association
inputs.searched_for: interaction term test statistic, df, or p-value

findings.reproduction: manual inspection of Methods, Tables 2 and 3, and Results - no CLI verb applies
findings.notes: The paper's central claim is moderation - title, Key Points and Conclusions all rest on veteran status changing the disability-suicide association. The Methods state an interaction term was fitted, but NO test of that interaction (statistic, df or p) appears anywhere in the article. What the tables report are simple-effect contrasts within strata. Inferring moderation from a significant contrast in one stratum and a non-significant one in another is the difference-in-significance fallacy: the >=3-limitation stratum's intervals are wide enough to be compatible with the same effect seen at 2 limitations (see absence_of_evidence_3plus_limitations). The interaction p-value is the quantity that would settle this and it is not reported. Rulebook rule 5.

findings.notes: The phrase 'test-specific significance levels' is an explicit statement that no multiplicity adjustment was made. Tables 2 and 3 alone contain 50 odds-ratio contrasts at alpha = .05, plus roughly 50 more in the cited sensitivity eTables and 18 baseline comparisons. Several headline findings sit close to the threshold - Table 3's 0.49 (p = .04, CI recovering .0453), 1.61 (p = .04, CI recovering .0344), and Table 2's 1.50 (1.01 to 2.23, p = .04) whose lower bound is 1.01 - and would not survive even a modest correction. This does not make any individual number wrong; it bears on how many of the 50 should be believed.

findings.location: Methods, Statistical Analysis
findings.quote: Analyses were conducted using SAS, version 9.4 (SAS Institute), which accommodated the complex NSDUH survey design and nonresponses by using PROC SURVEY procedures

inputs.searched_for: a-priori power analysis, target effect size, alpha, target power, minimum detectable effect

findings.reproduction: manual inspection of Methods - verify_power_analysis was deliberately NOT run
findings.notes: No a-priori power or precision calculation is reported. For a secondary analysis of a fixed existing survey that is defensible - the N was not under the authors' control - but it means the small-cell strata carry no stated minimum detectable effect. This matters most for the veteran subgroups: veterans are 13 859 unweighted respondents, and the >=3-limitation attempt cells are very small, the likely source of the wide intervals (e.g. 1.13 to 5.82) that drive the moderation claim. The authors themselves note 'smaller cell sizes after stratifying sample groups to veteran and nonveterans'. Recorded as a reporting gap, deliberately not forced through the tool.

findings.location: Table 1, P value column (18 baseline comparisons)
findings.quote: All evaluated covariates had significant bivariate associations (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 1) and were included in adjusted analyses.
findings.reproduction: csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were deliberately NOT run - no CLI command was issued
findings.notes: Deliberate non-check, and an important one. The Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher test and Table-1 dispersion analysis presuppose random allocation, under which baseline p-values should be Uniform(0,1) and uniformly HIGH p-values are the red flag. Here the comparison is veterans vs nonveterans - two naturally occurring populations that genuinely differ on essentially everything, at n = 231 099. Sixteen of eighteen rows at P<.001 is the expected result of a large-sample observational comparison, not a similarity anomaly, and running CSF would have inverted its logic. Rulebook rule 1 applies only to randomized designs.

findings.reproduction: grim_percentage, grimmer_check, sprite_reconstruct and debit_check were deliberately NOT run - no CLI command was issued
findings.notes: Deliberate non-check covering the largest family of numbers in the paper. Every percentage in Table 1 is a design-weighted estimate: the numerator is a sum of person-level survey weights, so it is not an integer count and the GRIM granularity argument does not hold. The paper also reports no means or SDs of any integer-scaled variable anywhere, so GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT have no valid target either. This is why the sweep's weight fell on check_estimate_ci and check_summation - the correct tools for a paper built from odds ratios and weighted counts.

unchecked.location: Table 1, P value column (18 baseline comparisons)
unchecked.reason: The authors do not state which test produced these p-values (design-based Rao-Scott chi-squared and Wald F are both plausible under PROC SURVEYFREQ), and only thresholded values are printed for 16 of 18 rows. Without the test type, cell counts, or exact p-values, no recalculation is possible. csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were separately ruled out as inapplicable to a non-randomized design.

unchecked.location: Table 2, AME (95% CI) column, all 30 cells
unchecked.reason: Printed to 2 decimals on values of magnitude <= 0.03, with twelve cells reading exactly '0 (0 to 0)' or similar. The rounding destroys the resolution that midpoint and p-recovery checks require; running them would generate spurious flags rather than information.

No validated tool performs a ratio recomputation from a weighted numerator and denominator, and grim_percentage is inapplicable to weighted survey estimates. Both numerators and the denominator were independently confirmed by check_summation; only the final division is unverified.

unchecked.location: Headline effect size versus field benchmarks
unchecked.reason: check_effect_plausibility requires a Cohen's d or group means/SDs/ns. This paper reports only odds ratios from a multinomial model with no group-level summary statistics, so no d can be formed and no field benchmark comparison is possible without inventing inputs.
